The dot product measures the 'similarity of direction' between two vectors. When vectors point in the same direction, the dot product is maximum (positive). When they are perpendicular, it is zero. When they point in opposite directions, it is minimum (negative).
Component of force: The component of force F along direction d is (F · d)/|d|
Normal vector: The dot product is used to find the normal to a plane: n · (r − r₀) = 0
Law of Cosines: The dot product gives a compact proof of the law of cosines: |b−a|² = |a|² + |b|² − 2|a||b|cos θ
Orthogonal decomposition: Any vector b can be decomposed into a component parallel to a and a component perpendicular to a: b = projab + (b − projab)
confusion: Do not confuse the dot product (scalar result) with the cross product (vector result). The dot product gives a number; the cross product gives a vector.
The dot product of two non-zero vectors can be zero even though neither vector is zero. This means the vectors are perpendicular, NOT that they are parallel.
When computing the projection, remember: the scalar projection is a number, while the vector projection is a vector in the direction of the reference vector.
The angle θ in a · b = |a| |b| cos θ is the ANGLE between the two vectors when placed tail-to-tail. Do not use the angle between head-to-tail arrangement.
If a · b = a · c, you CANNOT conclude that b = c. The dot product does not satisfy the cancellation law.

A positive dot product does NOT mean the vectors are parallel — it only means the angle is acute (less than 90°). The maximum dot product occurs when vectors are parallel and point in the same direction.

universalFacts: The dot product is also called the 'scalar product' because it produces a scalar (real number), not a vector.
The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality states: |a · b| ≤ |a| |b|, with equality if and only if the vectors are parallel.
The parallelogram law relates the dot product to magnitudes: |a + b|² + |a − b|² = 2(|a|² + |b|²).
In quantum mechanics, the dot product (inner product) is fundamental to calculating probability amplitudes and expectation values.
The dot product is the foundation of the concept of 'angle' in abstract vector spaces, leading to the definition of inner product spaces.
